scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that backs breadth while arguing for flexibility so depth is not crowded out; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Most universities ask students to take some classes far removed from their chosen major.
Some people recommend that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside their own field of study.
I largely agree that such breadth benefits students, though I believe the requirement should allow some flexibility.
First, studying outside one's main field makes students more rounded and capable thinkers.
Courses in different subjects expose students to new ideas, methods, and ways of seeing the world.
For example, an engineering student who studies history or ethics may make wiser decisions about how her work affects people.
This shows that broad knowledge helps students connect their speciality to the wider world.
Studying widely also builds flexible skills, such as writing and reasoning, that are useful in almost any career.
Many students, moreover, discover unexpected interests and even new career paths through courses they would never have chosen alone.
For these reasons, requiring some breadth is plainly good for students.
Second, however, such a requirement should be applied with care rather than rigidly forced on everyone.
Students already carry heavy workloads, and too many unrelated courses can crowd out the deep study their field demands.
Consider a medical student whose time is so limited that extra required courses leave too little room for essential training.
Forcing wide breadth in such cases could weaken the very expertise a university is meant to build.
A wiser policy lets students choose their outside courses from a broad menu rather than dictating each one.
Some flexibility also respects the fact that students differ in their goals and in the time they can spare.
Breadth works best, then, when it is encouraged and guided rather than rigidly imposed.
In conclusion, universities are right to want their students to study beyond their own field.
But the requirement should be flexible enough not to crowd out the depth that each subject needs.
The best policy gives students broad horizons while still protecting the focus their main field demands.
